title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XXXVIII: The Barrow Promised (lines 2752–2820)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 103–106, lines 2752–2820 (fitt XXXVIII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Ðā ic snūde gefrægn sunu Wīhstānes
æfter wordcwydum wundum dryhtne
hȳran heaðosīocum, hringnet beran,
brogdne beadusercean under beorges hrōf.
sentences.l: Then I swiftly heard that Wīhstān’s son, in accordance with word-sayings, obeyed the wounded lord, battle-sick, and bore the ring-net, the woven battle-shirt, under the barrow’s roof.
sentences.i: Then, as I quickly heard, Wīhstān’s son did as his wounded lord had told him, that lord sick with battle, and carried the mail, the woven war-shirt, in under the roof of the barrow.
sentences.n: The pattern is ‘ic … gefrægn’, ‘I heard’, followed by an accusative (‘sunu Wīhstānes’, ‘Wīhstān’s son’) and two infinitives, ‘hȳran’ (‘obey’, taking the dative ‘dryhtne’) and ‘beran’ (‘carry’). The son of Wīhstān is Wīglāf, whom the dying Beowulf has just sent in (‘Wīglāf lēofa’, 2745, in the last part). ‘æfter wordcwydum’ is ‘in accordance with the word-sayings’, that is, the instructions Beowulf gave; ‘æfter’ with the dative can mean ‘according to’. ‘wundum dryhtne heaðosīocum’ is ‘the wounded lord, battle-sick’ (‘heaðo’ ‘battle’ + ‘sēoc’ ‘sick’), both adjectives in the dative to agree with ‘dryhtne’. ‘hringnet’ is ‘ring-net’, the house word for mail, and ‘beadusercean’ is ‘battle-shirt’ (‘beadu’ ‘battle’ + ‘serce’ ‘shirt’), both accusative and in apposition. ‘brogdne’ is the past participle of ‘bregdan’ (‘weave, draw’), ‘woven’, and I take it as agreeing with ‘beadusercean’. ‘Serce’ is a feminine noun, and the feminine accusative singular of this participle is ‘brogdene’, which loses its middle vowel and is written ‘brogdne’ (as ‘gebunden’ gives ‘gebundne’), so the ending only looks masculine; the masculine accusative would be the longer ‘brogdenne’. The form does not suit neuter ‘hringnet’ (that would be ‘brogden’), so ‘woven’ goes with the shirt. The ‘n’ of ‘under’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘urder’, which makes no sense, and Thorkelin’s copy read ‘under’, which Klaeber follows. ‘beorges hrōf’ is ‘the barrow’s roof’, the vault of the dragon’s earth-hall.

sentences.t:
Geseah ðā sigehrēðig, þā hē bī sesse gēong,
magoþegn mōdig māððụmsigla fealo,
gold glitinian grunde getenge,
wundur on wealle, ond þæs wyrmes denn,
ealdes ūhtflogan, orcas stondan,
fyrnmanna fatu, feormendlēase,
hyrstum behrorene;
sentences.l: Then the brave young-thane saw, victory-glorious, when he went by the seat, many treasure-jewels, gold glittering close to the ground, wonder on the wall, and the worm’s den, the old dawn-flier’s, cups standing, vessels of men of old, without polishers, bereft of adornments;
sentences.i: Triumphant, the brave young man saw, as he passed the seat, many jewels of treasure, gold glittering close to the ground, marvels on the wall, and the den of the dragon, that old dawn-flier: cups standing about, the vessels of men long dead, with none to polish them, stripped of their ornaments;
sentences.n: ‘Geseah’ is the main verb and stands first; its subject (‘magoþegn mōdig’, ‘the brave young-thane’, Wīglāf) is held back to the next line, and the literal line puts it before the verb so that English can read it; everything after it is an accusative object, and ‘glitinian’ (‘glitter’) and ‘stondan’ (‘stand’) are infinitives, ‘saw gold glitter … saw cups stand’. ‘māððụmsigla’ is ‘treasure-jewels’ (‘sigle’, a jewel or brooch), and the dot under the ‘ụ’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, so it is not sounded as a full syllable in scanning the line. ‘fealo’ is Klaeber’s form of ‘many’; Kemble and others print ‘fela’, and Rieger and Sedgefield ‘feola’, with the same sense. ‘bī sesse’ is ‘by the seat’ (‘sess’ ‘seat, bench’): I take it to be a ledge or bench of stone at the barrow, perhaps the one Beowulf sat on at 2717 in the last part, and that is a guess. ‘sigehrēðig’ is ‘victory-glorious, triumphant’, as in fitt 23. ‘ond þæs wyrmes denn’ is ‘and the worm’s den’; Trautmann, Holthausen and Sedgefield read ‘geond’, ‘throughout’, in place of ‘ond’. ‘ealdes ūhtflogan’ is ‘of the old dawn-flier’, a genitive depending on ‘denn’; ‘ūht’ is the dark before dawn, when the dragon raids (compare the house word ‘ūhtsceaða’, dawn-scather). Klaeber prints ‘orcas’ for the cups: it is a loan from Latin ‘orca’, ‘jar’, and I take it as ‘cups’. Editors differ over the verb, ‘stōdan’ for ‘stondan’ (Ettmüller and others). ‘fyrnmanna fatu’ is ‘vessels of men of old’, and ‘feormendlēase’ is ‘without polishers’ (‘feormend’ ‘one who burnishes’ + ‘-lēas’), so the cups are tarnished and nobody cleans them. ‘hyrstum behrorene’ is ‘bereft of adornments’: ‘behrorene’ is the past participle of ‘behrēosan’, ‘fall away (from), be deprived of’, which takes the dative, and it agrees with ‘orcas’ and ‘fatu’, so it is the vessels that have lost their fittings; the gold has dropped off them.

sentences.t:
þǣr wæs helm monig
eald ond ōmig, earmbēaga fela
searwum gesǣled. —
sentences.l: There was many a helmet, old and rusty, many arm-rings skilfully bound. —
sentences.i: There was many a helmet, old and rusted, and many arm-rings cunningly bound. —
sentences.n: ‘þǣr wæs helm monig’ is ‘there was many a helmet’ (‘monig’ with a singular noun means ‘many a’), and ‘earmbēaga fela’ is ‘many of arm-rings’ (‘fela’ takes a genitive plural). ‘eald ond ōmig’ is ‘old and rusty’. ‘searwum gesǣled’ is ‘skilfully bound’: ‘gesǣled’ is the past participle of ‘gesǣlan’, ‘fasten, bind’, and ‘searwum’ a dative plural, ‘with cunning devices’; the rings are clasped or twisted in clever work. I do not know exactly what the binding is, and the sense of ‘fastened together in skilful work’ is a guess. The dash that ends this unit opens a remark the poet drops in aside; it is closed in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Sinc ēaðe mæg,
gold on grund(e) gumcynnes gehwone
oferhīgian, hȳde sē ðe wylle! —
sentences.l: Treasure, gold in the ground, may easily overpower each one of mankind; hide it, he who will! —
sentences.i: Treasure, gold lying in the earth, can easily get the better of any man alive; let him hide it who will! —
sentences.n: These three lines are a parenthetical aside in the poet’s own voice, set between dashes, a general saying (‘gnomic’: a statement of how things always are) breaking into the story. ‘Sinc’ and ‘gold’ are in apposition as the subject, ‘gumcynnes gehwone’ (‘each one of mankind’, the genitive depending on ‘gehwone’) is the object, and ‘mæg … oferhīgian’ is ‘may overpower’. ‘oferhīgian’ is hard, and I treat it as a guess: the root seems to be ‘hīgian’ ‘strive’, so ‘strive over’ and so ‘overpower’. Editors have proposed ‘-hȳdgian’ (Kluge), ‘-hīdgian’ (Schücking), ‘-hīwian’ (Grundtvig, with a query, and Sedgefield’s first edition) and, in Sedgefield’s second edition, the two words ‘ofer hige hēan’, so the word is not settled. The ‘e’ in parentheses in ‘grund(e)’ is Klaeber’s sign for a letter lost from the fire-damaged manuscript; his apparatus credits Grundtvig for it (‘Gru. tr.’). ‘hȳde sē ðe wylle’ is a wish or permission, ‘let him hide it, he who will’, with the subjunctive ‘hȳde’ and ‘sē ðe’ meaning ‘he who’; I take the point to be that hiding the gold in the earth does not save the hider, since the gold has the better of him. That is an interpretation, not a statement the Old English makes.

sentences.l: Likewise he saw hang a banner all-golden, high over the hoard, greatest of hand-wonders, locked by limb-crafts;
sentences.i: He saw also a banner of pure gold hanging high above the hoard, the greatest of marvels wrought by hand, interlaced with skilled craft;
sentences.n: ‘Swylce’ is ‘likewise, moreover’, and ‘siomian’ is an infinitive, ‘hang’, after ‘geseah’, ‘saw a banner hang’. ‘segn eallgylden’ is ‘banner all-golden’, a standard of gold throughout (what it was made of beyond that is not said); ‘hondwundra mǣst’ is ‘greatest of hand-wonders’, a partitive genitive plural after the superlative. ‘gelocen’ is the past participle of ‘lūcan’, ‘lock, fasten together’, so ‘locked, interwoven’, and ‘leoðocræftum’ is a dative plural and a compound found only here. I read it as ‘limb-crafts’ (‘liþ’, the word for a limb or joint, + ‘cræft’), crafts of the joints or fingers, that is, skilled handiwork; the same first element is in ‘leoðosyrcan’, ‘limb-corslet’, at 1505 and 1890; that is a guess, and other scholars have taken the first half to be ‘lēoþ’, ‘song’, and understood magic craft, spells sung over the weave.

sentences.t:
of ðām lēoma stōd,
þæt hē þone grundwong ongitan meahte,
wrǣte giondwlītan. Næs ðæs wyrmes þǣr
onsȳn ǣnig, ac hyne ecg fornam.
sentences.l: from which a light stood, so that he could perceive the ground-plain and look over the jewels. There was not of the worm there any sight, but the edge took him off.
sentences.i: From it a light shone out, so that he could make out the floor of the chamber and look over the jewels. Of the dragon there was no sign at all, but the sword had carried him off.
sentences.n: ‘of ðām lēoma stōd’ is ‘from which a ray stood’ (a light stood out, shone). Klaeber prints the ‘a’ of ‘lēoma’ in italic: the manuscript has ‘leoman’, and Kemble’s ‘lēoma’ is followed. ‘þæt hē … ongitan meahte’ is a result clause, ‘so that he could perceive’, with the infinitive ‘ongitan’ and a second, ‘giondwlītan’ (‘look over’). The object ‘wrǣte’ is an accusative plural, ‘jewels, ornaments’ (‘wrǣt’); Klaeber’s ‘te’ is in italic because the manuscript has ‘wræce’, which would be ‘vengeance, exile’ and gives no sense, and Thorpe’s ‘wrǣte’ is followed. ‘grundwong’ is ‘ground-plain’, the floor of the chamber. The next sentence turns on the negative ‘Næs … ǣnig’, ‘there was not … any’, with ‘ðæs wyrmes’ a genitive after ‘onsȳn’ (‘sight’); and ‘ac’ is ‘but’, not ‘for’: ‘hyne ecg fornam’ has ‘ecg’, ‘edge’, as subject, the sword being the thing named for its cutting side, and ‘fornam’ ‘took away, destroyed’. The dragon’s body is no longer to be seen: I take it that the dragon has been killed, and that nothing of it lies there; the poet does not say what became of the body.

sentences.t:
Ðā ic on hlǣwe gefrægn hord rēafian,
eald enta geweorc ānne mannan,
him on bearm hladon bunan ond discas
sylfes dōme;
sentences.l: Then I heard that in the barrow one man plundered the hoard, the old work of giants, loaded into his lap cups and dishes at his own judgement;
sentences.i: Then, so I heard, one man alone plundered the hoard in the barrow, that ancient work of giants, and loaded cups and dishes into his lap as he saw fit;
sentences.n: ‘Ðā ic … gefrægn’ is the ‘I heard’ formula again, with an accusative and infinitive: ‘I heard one man plunder the hoard’ (‘ānne mannan’ is the accusative, ‘hord rēafian’ the infinitive phrase). ‘eald enta geweorc’ is ‘old work of giants’, in apposition to ‘hord’: in this poem ancient buried things (swords, buildings, hoards) are called the work of ‘ents’, a race of giants, because they are older than anyone can say. The verb ‘hladon’ is hard. The manuscript has ‘hlodon’ (‘they loaded’, past plural) and Klaeber changes the vowel to ‘a’, printing ‘hladon’ with the italic ‘a’; Grundtvig and Sedgefield read ‘hladan’, an infinitive. I take it as an infinitive in line with ‘rēafian’, ‘plunder … and load’ (as at 2126, where ‘hladan’ is an infinitive); the ending ‘-on’ for ‘-an’ is irregular, so this is a guess about what Klaeber intends. ‘him on bearm’ is ‘into his lap’ (‘bearm’ ‘bosom, lap’; the ‘him’ is the dative of the man), ‘bunan’ is ‘cups’ (the word occurs rarely and I take the sense ‘drinking vessels’), and ‘discas’ ‘dishes’. ‘sylfes dōme’ is ‘at his own judgement’, that is, as he chose. I take the man to be Wīglāf, and the word ‘rēafian’ (‘plunder’) is the poem’s, though he acts on his lord’s command.

sentences.t:
segn ēac genōm,
bēacna beorhtost.
sentences.l: he took also the banner, brightest of beacons.
sentences.i: He took the banner too, brightest of all ensigns.
sentences.n: ‘genōm’ is the past of ‘geniman’, ‘take’, with the banner (‘segn’) as its object; the verb stands after ‘ēac’ (‘also’). ‘bēacna beorhtost’ is ‘brightest of beacons’, a superlative with a partitive genitive plural; ‘bēacen’ is any signal or sign, and here a banner seen from far.

sentences.t:
Bill ǣr gescọ̄d
— ecg wæs īren — ealdhlāfordes
þām ðāra māðma mundbora wæs
longe hwīle, līgegesan wæg
hātne for horde, hioroweallende
middelnihtum, oð þæt hē morðre swealt.
sentences.l: The sword of the old lord — its edge was iron — had before harmed the one who was, for a long while, protector of those treasures, who bore fire-terror, hot, before the hoard, surging with swords in the middle of nights, until he died in slaughter.
sentences.i: The sword of the old lord — its edge was iron — had earlier wounded the creature who for a long time had been guardian of that treasure, and who had borne hot fire-terror before the hoard, surging as if with swords at midnight, night after night, until he died by violence.
sentences.n: The main clause is ‘Bill ǣr gescọ̄d ealdhlāfordes þām … mundbora’: ‘bill’ is the subject, ‘ealdhlāfordes’ depends on it (‘the old lord’s sword’), and ‘gescọ̄d’ is the past of ‘sceððan’, ‘harm, injure’, which takes the dative: ‘þām’ is that dative, ‘to him (who)’, and ‘ðāra māðma mundbora wæs’ says who he was, with ‘mundbora’ the nominative (‘protector’), the predicate of ‘wæs’. The dot under the vowel of ‘gescọ̄d’ is the same sign as before, Klaeber’s mark that the vowel does not count in the metre. I take the ‘old lord’ to be Beowulf, and the sword to be the one that struck the dragon in the last fight, whichever one that was. Two other readings exist: Kemble and others read ‘ǣrgescōd’ as one word, ‘brass-shod’ (the sword shod with brass, though the next words say the edge was iron), and Rieger, the Dutch Aantekeningen and Sedgefield read the dative ‘ealdhlāforde’, ‘the old lord’, meaning the dragon. ‘ecg wæs īren’ is a parenthesis, ‘its edge was iron’. ‘mundbora’ is ‘protector’ (‘mund’ ‘protection’ + ‘bora’ ‘bearer’) and ‘longe hwīle’ ‘for a long while’. ‘līgegesan’ is ‘fire-terror’ (‘līg’ ‘flame’ + ‘egesa’ ‘terror’), the object of ‘wæg’ (‘bore, carried on’), with ‘hātne’ ‘hot’ to agree. ‘hioroweallende’ is a guess: ‘weallende’ is ‘welling, surging’ and ‘hioro-’ is ‘sword’, so the literal sense is ‘surging with swords’, perhaps a fury like a battle’s; the idiomatic line keeps that image. ‘morðre swealt’ is ‘died in slaughter’ (dative ‘morðre’, ‘murder, violent death’).

sentences.t:
Ār wæs on ofoste, eftsīðes georn,
frætwum gefyrðred;
sentences.l: The messenger was in haste, eager for the return journey, furthered with treasures;
sentences.i: The messenger was in haste, eager to be on his way back, laden with treasures;
sentences.n: ‘Ār’ is ‘messenger’, a nominative (it can also mean ‘honour’, but Klaeber’s glossary gives ‘messenger, herald’ and that fits, as at 335 in fitt 5); the messenger is Wīglāf, who is hurrying back to his dying lord with the treasure. ‘on ofoste’ is ‘in haste’, and ‘eftsīðes georn’ is ‘eager of the return journey’ (‘georn’ takes a genitive). ‘gefyrðred’ is a past participle of ‘fyrðran’, ‘further, advance’; the sense ‘furthered with treasures’, meaning loaded, is a guess from that, and the word is found only here.

sentences.t:
hyne fyrwet bræc,
hwæðer collenferð cwicne gemētte
in ðām wongstede Wedra þēoden
ellensīocne, þǣr hē hine ǣr forlēt.
sentences.l: curiosity broke him, whether the swollen-minded one would find the Weders’ prince living in that plain-place, sick in his strength, where he had left him before.
sentences.i: He was tormented by wondering whether he, bold of heart, would find the prince of the Weders alive in that open place, though sick in his strength, where he had left him.
sentences.n: ‘hyne fyrwet bræc’ is ‘curiosity broke him’: ‘fyrwet’ (‘curiosity, anxious wondering’) is the subject and ‘bræc’ ‘afflicted, tormented’. The wondering is a ‘hwæðer’ clause, ‘whether he would find’, with ‘gemētte’ a past subjunctive (the weak past singular looks the same in the indicative, and the indirect question decides). ‘collenferð’ is a guess, ‘swollen-minded’ in the literal line and ‘bold of heart’ in the idiomatic one, as at 1806 in fitt 25 (‘collen’ seems to be ‘swollen, excited’, so ‘proud, eager’, + ‘ferhð’ ‘mind’), and I take it as nominative, a description of Wīglāf; Ettmüller read it as accusative, ‘-ferðne’, going with the prince. ‘cwicne’ is ‘living’ and ‘ellensīocne’ ‘sick in his strength’ (‘ellen’ ‘courage, strength’ + ‘sēoc’), both accusative to agree with ‘Wedra þēoden’, the Weders’ prince, that is Beowulf. ‘wongstede’ is ‘plain-place’ (‘wong’ ‘field’ + ‘stede’ ‘place’), the open ground by the barrow wall, where he had left Beowulf sitting (2715 in the last part). ‘þǣr hē hine ǣr forlēt’ is ‘where he had left him before’, the first ‘hē’ being Wīglāf and ‘hine’ Beowulf.

sentences.l: He then, with the treasures, found the famed prince, his lord, bloody, at the end of his life;
sentences.i: Carrying the treasures, he found the famed prince, his lord, covered in blood and at the end of his life;
sentences.n: ‘fand’ is the verb, with two accusatives in apposition (‘mǣrne þīoden’ and ‘dryhten sīnne’) and the adjective ‘drīorigne’ (‘bloody, gory’) agreeing with them. ‘mid þām māðmum’ is ‘with the treasures’, which Wīglāf is carrying. ‘ealdres æt ende’ is ‘at the end of life’ (‘ealdor’ here is ‘life’, genitive), a phrase meaning that Beowulf is at the point of death.

sentences.t:
hē hine eft ongon
wæteres weorpan, oð þæt wordes ord
brēosthord þurhbræc. [Biorncyning spræc]
gomel on giohðe — gold scēawode —:
sentences.l: he began again to throw water at him, until the point of a word broke through the breast-hoard. [The warrior-king spoke], old in sorrow — he looked on the gold —:
sentences.i: He set about sprinkling him with water once more, until the first word forced its way out of the treasure-house of his breast. The warrior-king spoke, old and sorrowing, looking on the gold:
sentences.n: ‘hē hine eft ongon wæteres weorpan’ is ‘he began again to throw (of) water at him’: ‘weorpan’ takes the genitive ‘wæteres’, a partitive, ‘some of the water’, so ‘sprinkle’; Kemble and others read the dative ‘wætere’, and Rieger and Trautmann ‘wætere sweorfan’, ‘rub with water’. ‘oð þæt’ is ‘until’; ‘wordes ord’ is ‘the point of a word’, the first word, the front edge of speech, and ‘brēosthord’ (‘breast-hoard’) is the breast as the treasure-store of thought, as ‘bānhūs’ and others are bodies. The square brackets in ‘[Biorncyning spræc]’ are Klaeber’s sign that these words are supplied by an editor and are not in the manuscript; the apparatus does not say what the manuscript has here, but the sentence and the verse both want a half-line. This is an emendation, restored by editors in several ways: Grundtvig and others restore ‘[Bēowulf maþelode]’, Schücking ‘[Þā se beorn gespræc]’ and Holthausen and Chambers ‘[Bīowulf reordode]’. ‘Biorncyning’ is ‘warrior-king’ (‘beorn’ is a warrior, as in ‘beorncyning’ at 2148 in fitt 31) and ‘spræc’ ‘spoke’. The ‘h’ of ‘giohðe’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘giogoðe’, ‘youth’, which would give ‘old in youth’, and Grimm and Ettmüller changed it to ‘giohðe’, ‘in sorrow’, which suits ‘gomel’ (‘old’) better. ‘gold scēawode’ is ‘he looked on the gold’ and sits between dashes, a side remark; the colon after the dash opens the speech.

sentences.t:
‘Ic ðāra frætwa Frēan ealles ðanc,
Wuldurcyninge wordum secge,
ēcum Dryhtne, þē ic hēr on starie,
þæs ðe ic mōste mīnum lēodum
ǣr swyltdæge swylc gestrȳnan.
sentences.l: ‘I say thanks in words, for these treasures, to the Lord of all, to the Glory-King, to the eternal Lord, on which (treasures) I here gaze, for that, that I was allowed for my people, before my death-day, to gain such a thing.
sentences.i: ‘I give thanks in words for these treasures, which I look on here, to the Lord of all, the King of glory, the everlasting Lord, because I was allowed to win such a thing for my people before the day of my death.
sentences.n: The main clause is ‘Ic … ðanc … secge’, ‘I say thanks’, with ‘ðāra frætwa’ (genitive plural) giving the thing thanked for and ‘Frēan ealles’, ‘Wuldurcyninge’ and ‘ēcum Dryhtne’ (all dative) the one thanked; ‘Frēa ealles’ is ‘Lord of all’, ‘Wuldurcyning’ ‘Glory-King’ (‘wuldor’ ‘glory’ + ‘cyning’), and ‘ēcum Dryhtne’ ‘to the eternal Lord’; the three are titles of God in the poem’s Christian voice. ‘þē ic hēr on starie’ is a relative clause, ‘on which I gaze here’, with ‘þē’ the relative particle pointing back to ‘frætwa’. Then ‘þæs ðe’ introduces the second ground, ‘for that, that’, followed by ‘mōste’ (past subjunctive of ‘mōtan’, ‘was allowed to’) and the infinitive ‘gestrȳnan’, ‘gain’, with ‘swylc’ ‘such a thing’ as object. ‘ǣr swyltdæge’ is ‘before death-day’, a compound of ‘swylt’ ‘death’ and ‘dæg’ in the dative. The single quote that opens this unit begins Beowulf’s speech.

sentences.t:
Nū ic on māðma hord mīne bebohte
frōde feorhlege, fremmað gēna
lēoda þearfe; ne mæg ic hēr leng wesan.
sentences.l: Now I have sold my old life-laying for the hoard of treasures; provide still for the need of the people; I may not be here longer.
sentences.i: Now that I have given my old life in exchange for this hoard of treasure, go on seeing to the needs of the people; I cannot stay here any longer.
sentences.n: ‘Nū ic … bebohte’ is ‘now I have sold’ (‘bebohte’, past of ‘bebycgan’, ‘sell’), and ‘on māðma hord’ is ‘in exchange for the hoard of treasures’; the thing sold is ‘mīne frōde feorhlege’, ‘my old life-laying’, which I take to mean the laying down of his life (‘feorh’ ‘life’ + ‘lege’ ‘lying, laying down’); ‘frōde’ is ‘old, wise’. The ‘ne’ of ‘mīne’ is in italic because the manuscript has ‘minne’, the masculine form, and Ettmüller changed it to ‘mīne’ to agree with ‘feorhlege’, which I take as feminine, as both ‘mīne’ and ‘frōde’ then fit. ‘fremmað gēna lēoda þearfe’ is hard: ‘fremmað’ is a plural imperative, ‘perform, carry out’, ‘gēna’ ‘still, further’ and ‘lēoda þearfe’ ‘the people’s need’. The form is plural, though Wīglāf alone stands before him (the next verb, ‘hātað’, is plural too). Thorpe, Bugge and most editors divide ‘gēna’ as ‘gē nū’, ‘you now’, which keeps the plural and only supplies the pronoun. A plural may address Wīglāf as spokesman for the people whose need the line names; that is a guess. I render it as a command, ‘provide still for’, not the statement ‘you still provide’, because Beowulf is giving a charge. ‘ne mæg ic hēr leng wesan’ is ‘I may not be here longer’.

sentences.t:
Hātað heaðomǣre hlǣw gewyrcean
beorhtne æfter bǣle æt brimes nōsan;
sentences.l: Bid the battle-famed make a barrow, bright, after the pyre, at the sea’s headland;
sentences.i: Bid the men famed in battle build a bright mound, when my body has been burned, on the headland by the sea;
sentences.n: ‘Hātað’ is a plural imperative, ‘bid, command’, with an accusative of the person (‘heaðomǣre’, ‘the battle-famed’, accusative plural) and an infinitive (‘gewyrcean’, ‘make’), and the object ‘hlǣw’, ‘barrow’, with ‘beorhtne’ ‘bright’; Sievers and Holthausen read ‘beorht’. ‘æfter bǣle’ is ‘after the pyre’, that is, after the burning of his body, since the dead hero is to be cremated. ‘æt brimes nōsan’ is ‘at the sea’s headland’ (‘nōse’ is ‘nose’, hence a promontory). The barrow is to be a seamark, and the next words name it.

sentences.t:
sē scel tō gemyndum mīnum lēodum
hēah hlīfian on Hronesnæsse,
þæt hit sǣlīðend syððan hātan
Bīowulfes biorh, ðā ðe brentingas
ofer flōda genipu feorran drīfað.’
sentences.l: it shall be for remembrances to my people, towering high on Hronesnæs, so that sea-farers may afterwards call it Beowulf’s barrow, those who drive the steep-ones over the mists of the floods from far.’
sentences.i: It shall stand as a memorial to my people, rising high on Hronesnæs, so that seafarers, those who steer their lofty ships from far across the mists of the waters, may call it Beowulf’s Barrow in the years to come.’
sentences.n: ‘sē scel’ is ‘it shall’, ‘sē’ being the masculine pronoun for the barrow (Sievers and Holthausen read neuter ‘þæt’ for it), and ‘tō gemyndum’ ‘for remembrances’, that is, as a memorial. ‘hlīfian’ is ‘tower, rise high’. ‘Hronesnæsse’ is a place name, in the dative: ‘næss’ is a headland and ‘Hrones’ is probably the genitive of ‘hron’, ‘whale’, so ‘Whale’s Ness’; it could instead be a personal name, and I cannot say, so I leave the name as printed. This is the headland in the Geats’ country where the barrow will be built. ‘þæt hit sǣlīðend syððan hātan’ is a purpose clause, ‘so that sea-farers (‘sǣ’ ‘sea’ + ‘līðend’ ‘goers’) may call it afterwards’, with the subjunctive ‘hātan’. ‘Bīowulfes biorh’ is ‘Beowulf’s barrow’. ‘brentingas’ appears only here: it is built on ‘brant’, ‘steep’, so ‘steep ones’, and since it is what sailors drive (‘drīfað’, ‘drive, urge on’) over the water I take it to be ‘high-prowed ships’; that is a guess. ‘flōda genipu’ is ‘the floods’ mists’ (‘genipu’, accusative plural, after ‘ofer’). The closing quotation mark ends the speech.

sentences.t:
Dyde him of healse hring gyldenne
þīoden þrīsthȳdig, þegne gesealde,
geongum gārwigan, goldfāhne helm,
bēah ond byrnan, hēt hyne brūcan well —:
sentences.l: The bold-minded prince took from his neck the golden ring and gave it to the thane, the young spear-warrior, and the gold-gleaming helm, ring and byrnie, and bade him enjoy them well —:
sentences.i: The bold-hearted prince took the golden ring from his neck and gave it to his thane, the young spearman, together with the gold-gleaming helmet, the ring and the mail-coat, and told him to make good use of them:
sentences.n: ‘Dyde him of healse’ is ‘took from himself off the neck’, ‘dōn of’ being ‘take off’ and ‘him’ a dative of the one who loses it. ‘þīoden þrīsthȳdig’ is ‘bold-minded prince’ (‘þrīst’ ‘bold’ + the stem of ‘hyge’, ‘mind’); ‘þegne gesealde’ is ‘gave to the thane’, and ‘geongum gārwigan’ ‘to the young spear-warrior’ (‘gār’ ‘spear’ + ‘wiga’ ‘warrior’, as Wīglāf is called at 2672); ‘goldfāhne helm’ ‘gold-gleaming helm’ (‘fāh’, ‘gleaming, variegated’, as ‘goldfāh’ was rendered of the hall in fitt 4), ‘bēah’ ‘ring’ (an arm-ring or neck-ring; it is not clear whether it is the same as the ‘hring gyldenne’, so I give it as a second item), and ‘byrnan’ ‘byrnie’. The objects come as a list after ‘gesealde’. ‘hēt hyne brūcan well’ is ‘bade him enjoy well’, with ‘hēt’ taking an accusative and infinitive; the colon after the dash opens the next speech.

sentences.t:
‘Þū eart endelāf ūsses cynnes,
Wǣgmundinga;
sentences.l: ‘You are the last remnant of our kin, of the Wǣgmundings;
sentences.i: ‘You are the last left of our family, the Wǣgmundings;
sentences.n: ‘endelāf’ is ‘end-leaving’ (‘ende’ ‘end’ + ‘lāf’ ‘what is left’), the last one remaining, and ‘ūsses cynnes’ ‘of our kin’ is a genitive. ‘Wǣgmundinga’ is a genitive plural in apposition, ‘of the Wǣgmundings’, the family of Wīglāf and, as Beowulf says ‘our’, of Beowulf himself; the name is formed from a forefather ‘Wǣgmund’. The speech opens with the quotation mark.

sentences.l: fate swept away all my kinsmen to the Measurer’s decree, earls in courage;
sentences.i: fate has swept all my kinsmen away to their appointed end, the earls in their valour;
sentences.n: ‘wyrd’ is ‘fate’, the subject, and ‘ealle’ is an accusative plural that goes with ‘māgas’, ‘kinsmen’, the object, not with ‘wyrd’ (so ‘fate … all my kinsmen’, with the words far apart); ‘forswēop’ is ‘swept away’ (the same verb is used of fate in the Grendel story, fitt 7). The letters ‘wēop’ are in italic: the manuscript has ‘speof’, and Kemble’s ‘-swēop’ is followed. On the printed page the ‘w’ and ‘p’ are clearly italic and the ‘ēo’ only possibly (that is the transcriber’s reading of the page, not Klaeber’s apparatus). ‘tō metodsceafte’ is ‘to the Measurer’s decree’: ‘metod’ is God, ‘the Measurer’, and ‘sceaft’ ‘ordinance, creation’, so it means they were taken to the death that God had appointed. ‘eorlas on elne’ is ‘earls in courage’, in apposition to ‘māgas’.

sentences.t: ic him æfter sceal.’
sentences.l: I must after them.’
sentences.i: I must follow them.’
sentences.n: ‘ic him æfter sceal’ has ‘sceal’ (‘must, shall’) with no verb of motion, which Old English leaves out after verbs like ‘sculan’; the sense is ‘I must go after them’. ‘him’ is a dative plural, ‘them’ (the dead kinsmen), with ‘æfter’ coming after it. The closing quotation mark ends Beowulf’s speech.

sentences.l: That was to the old man the last word from breast-thoughts, before he chose the pyre, the hot battle-surges;
sentences.i: That was the old man’s last word, out of the thoughts of his heart, before he chose the funeral pyre, with its hot flames surging like battle;
sentences.n: ‘Þæt wæs þām gomelan gingæste word’ is ‘that was to the old man the last word’ (‘þām gomelan’, dative, ‘for the old man’; ‘gingæste’ is the superlative of ‘geong’, ‘young’, and means ‘last’, the youngest, latest). ‘brēostgehygdum’ is a dative plural, ‘from breast-thoughts’ (‘brēost’ ‘breast’ + ‘gehygd’ ‘thought’), the instrument of the word. ‘ǣr hē bǣl cure’ is ‘before he chose the pyre’ (‘cure’ the past subjunctive of ‘cēosan’, ‘choose’): he chooses it in the sense that he accepts it as his death. ‘hāte heaðowylmas’ is in apposition to ‘bǣl’, ‘the hot battle-surges’ (‘heaðo’ ‘battle’ + ‘wylm’ ‘surge, billow’), which I take to be the flames of the pyre. The compound is odd, since it names the pyre by the word for war, and I am not sure that the flames of the pyre, and not the dragon’s fire that killed him, are meant.

sentences.t:
him of hræðre gewāt
sāwol sēcean sōðfæstra dōm.
sentences.l: from his breast went the soul to seek the doom of the truth-fast.
sentences.i: From his breast the soul went forth to seek the judgement of the righteous.
sentences.n: ‘him of hræðre gewāt sāwol’ is ‘from him, from the breast, departed the soul’ (‘him’ a dative of the one who loses it, and ‘hræðre’ the dative of ‘hrǣðer’, ‘breast’). The ‘r’ of ‘hræðre’ is in italic: the manuscript has ‘hwæðre’, which would be ‘however’ or ‘whether’; Kemble and others read ‘hreðre’, and Grein’s dictionary ‘hræðre’, which Klaeber follows. ‘sēcean’ is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to seek’. ‘sōðfæstra dōm’ is ‘the doom of the truth-fast’, that is, of the righteous (‘sōð’ ‘truth’ + ‘fæst’ ‘fixed’, with a genitive plural). ‘dōm’ means both ‘judgement’ and ‘glory’, and I cannot tell which the poet wants: either the soul goes to be judged among the righteous, or to share their glory.
